IB 2027 | SL | Unit 1

B1.1 Problem Specification

Define the problem before writing the solution

Cluster A | Frame the problem

What is missing from this request?

"Build a canteen app so lunch queues disappear."

What must we clarify before any algorithm design starts?

I do

Model a full problem specification

Component Modeled example
Problem statement Queue time averages 14 minutes and wrong orders are common.
Objectives Reduce queue time under 5 minutes and lower order errors to near zero.
Constraints Budget is limited, offline mode required, allergy compliance required.
Input / output Input: meal choice + student ID. Output: kitchen ticket + confirmation screen.
Evaluation criteria Success is measured by queue timing and mismatch logs.

We do

Classify the statements

Sort these into the correct parts of a problem specification:

  • "Must run on existing tablets."
  • "Staff need fewer manual steps."
  • "Average order confirmation under 10 seconds."
  • "Output includes allergy warning."

You do

Worksheet handoff

You Do: Complete the B1.1 specification worksheet in the Activities section.

Draft a full problem specification from a short school scenario.

Cluster B | Stakeholder tension

Whose success counts most?

The same system can serve students, staff, and finance teams differently.

How do we design when stakeholder priorities conflict?

I do

Build a stakeholder map

Stakeholder Priority Risk if ignored
Students Fast ordering and reliable output Abandonment and queue crowding
Canteen staff Accurate tickets and clear output flow Order rework and delays
School leaders Cost control and compliance constraints Budget overrun or legal issue

We do

Negotiate trade-offs

If budget blocks a new scanner, what changes first:

  • Interface speed target
  • Report detail in output
  • Number of optional features

Defend the choice using stakeholder impact, not preference.

You do

Worksheet handoff

You Do: Complete the stakeholder conflict worksheet in the Activities section.

Prioritize stakeholder needs and justify one compromise.

Cluster C | Precision

When is a goal too vague to test?

"Make the app better" cannot be verified.

How do constraints, input, output, and measurable evaluation criteria make success testable?

I do

Rewrite vague targets

Weak statement Improved statement
The UI is good. 80% of students complete order input in under 45 seconds.
System is reliable. Failed transactions remain below 1% over one week.
Output is clear. Kitchen output includes meal, allergens, and timestamp every order.

We do

Improve this requirement set

Take the statement below and make it testable:

"The platform should work globally."

Specify at least one language constraint, one legal constraint, one input standard, and one measurable evaluation criteria metric.

Synthesis

What would fail first if we skipped the problem specification stage?

Would the first breakdown happen in stakeholder alignment, constraints handling, or success measurement? Explain why.
